title: The Last Interior
premise: Petra Eastwick, a literary translator raised between two languages, returns to her family's condemned house to sort her mother's effects and discovers an inventory notebook cataloguing everything the family never said aloud. A stranger named Tomas appears at the funeral claiming the family once knew him under a name no one uses anymore — a name from Petra's fading childhood language. As demolition day approaches, Petra and Tomas decode the notebook's final, untranslatable sentence, which reveals what her mother actually chose to keep silent about: the child she gave away, the life she invented to survive it. In the end, Petra translates the sentence not into words but into an act — she opens the house's doors one last time, lets the found family of neighbors and strangers walk through it, and carries the language forward by teaching it to someone new.
about_author: Xanthe Eastwick is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up trilingual in a port town and now writes about the words families lose on purpose. She lives near a river that changes its name every century, and this is her second novel.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Petra, first-person POV, arrives at the house three days before the funeral and finds her mother's notebook: a meticulous list of sentences never spoken, each dated. She recognizes her own handwriting in the margins from childhood. Emotional beat: grief sharpened into curiosity; the reader learns Petra is losing her mother tongue word by word.

chapters.title: A Stranger Knows the Name
chapters.summary: At the funeral, a man in a borrowed coat calls the family by 'the Vessin name' — a word Petra hasn't heard since she was nine. Her aunt goes white; her brother walks out. Petra follows the stranger, Tomas, into the churchyard. POV alternates briefly to Tomas for the first time. Beat: the sealed past cracks open.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Petra lets Tomas into the house because he claims he lived in it as a boy, before the family changed names. He points to things only a resident would know — the doorframe notches, the hidden cold pantry. Petra checks the inventory notebook against his claims. Beat: uneasy alliance formed over shared, unverifiable memory.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, quieter chapter. She works on a translation commission she can't finish and notices her childhood language slipping — she reaches for a word and finds only its shadow. Flashbacks to her mother refusing to speak it at home. Beat: the stakes become personal and linguistic, not just familial.

chapters.title: The Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: The city posts the official date: six weeks. The brother, Daniel, wants to sign immediately and take the payout; Petra wants time. Their argument exposes old fault lines — who was favored, who was exiled. Beat: ticking clock established; sibling conflict becomes the story's second engine.

chapters.title: Tomas's Version
chapters.summary: Tomas tells his story: he was the neighbor's foster kid, taken in for one winter by Petra's mother, then sent away when 'the arrangement' ended. He remembers being called by a name that wasn't his own. Beat: tenderness and suspicion in equal measure; Petra can't tell if he's grieving or conning.

chapters.title: The Notebook's Gaps
chapters.summary: Petra discovers pages torn from the inventory notebook and matches the tear patterns to dates around her ninth year. Someone — her mother? her aunt? — removed the most important unsaid things. Beat: mystery deepens; the archive itself becomes untrustworthy.

chapters.title: Aunt Vera's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Petra visits Aunt Vera, who speaks the old language fluently but refuses to teach it, calling it 'a debt language.' Over stew, Vera almost says something about the winter Tomas describes, then stops herself mid-sentence. Beat: the cost of silence made visible in a living person.

chapters.title: Translation as Betrayal
chapters.summary: Petra's professional life intrudes: her client rejects her translation as 'too faithful.' A meditation chapter on whether any sentence survives crossing between languages — or between people. She begins translating the inventory notebook privately. Beat: theme crystallizes; translation becomes the novel's central metaphor.

chapters.title: The Photograph Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Following Tomas's memory of the cold pantry, Petra pries up a board and finds a photograph: her mother, young, holding a baby that isn't Petra or Daniel, with a woman Petra doesn't recognize. On the back, one word in the old language. Beat: the untranslatable sentence takes physical form.

chapters.title: Daniel's Ledger
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. He's been keeping his own ledger — of money owed, favors unpaid, years unthanked. We see why he wants the house gone: it's the only way he knows to close the account. He confronts Petra about Tomas, accusing him of running a long game. Beat: Daniel humanized; threat of eviction accelerates.

chapters.title: The Word on the Back
chapters.summary: Petra brings the photograph to a dying speaker of the old language, Mrs. Ondrusek, at a care home. The word means something between 'kept,' 'held,' and 'owed' — no English equivalent. Mrs. Ondrusek recognizes the other woman in the photo and refuses, gently, to say more. Beat: revelation half-delivered; language shown as a locked room.

chapters.title: Six Weeks Becomes Five
chapters.summary: Petra petitions the city for a heritage review and fails. Daniel signs preliminary papers. Tomas offers to testify that the house has historical significance — he's been researching archives all along, which makes Petra wonder again what he really wants. Beat: pressure mounts; trust wobbles.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Vera finally talks, in fragments: Petra's mother took in a friend's baby during a bad winter — the woman in the photograph — and the 'arrangement' was that the child would be called by the family's old name until she could be claimed. She never was. The torn pages listed every day the mother didn't say goodbye. Beat: the secret's shape revealed; grief reframed as unfinished hospitality.

chapters.title: Whose Child Was Kept
chapters.summary: Petra realizes the baby may be alive, and that Tomas's timeline doesn't fit — he was the older foster boy who stayed the same winter. She confronts him; he admits he came looking for the girl, not the family, and lost track of her decades ago. Beat: betrayal and relief braided together; motive clarified.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Petra finds the final entry in the notebook, written the week before her mother's death: one long sentence in the old language, grammatically impossible, mixing tenses so it can't be cleanly translated. She sits with it for days. Beat: stillness before climax; the sentence becomes a mirror for everything the book has asked.

chapters.title: Mrs. Ondrusek's Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Petra reads the sentence aloud to Mrs. Ondrusek, who translates it not literally but truthfully: 'I kept what was given me, and I gave back nothing, and the keeping was the love.' The old woman dies two days later, taking more of the language with her. Beat: emotional peak of understanding; loss and clarity arrive together.

chapters.title: Finding Nadia
chapters.summary: Following the photograph and Vera's fragments, Petra locates the kept child — Nadia — working at a coastal cannery town, raised under another name entirely. Petra writes to her instead of arriving unannounced, choosing the sentence her mother never managed. Beat: courage expressed as restraint; the arc turns toward repair.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Nadia replies with one line: 'Show me the house.' Petra, Daniel, Tomas, and Vera gather on the last night, opening every door and window, reading the inventory entries aloud — some for the first time said. Daniel crosses out his ledger. Beat: catharsis; the house emptied of secrets before it's emptied of walls.

chapters.title: The Last Interior
chapters.summary: Climax. Nadia arrives at dawn. Inside, Petra reads her mother's untranslatable sentence aloud in the original language, then in her own translation, then hands Nadia the notebook and the photograph. The machines wait outside. Beat: the sentence is finally 'lived with' — spoken, witnessed, survived.

chapters.title: Rubble, Alphabet
chapters.summary: The house comes down. Petra watches without flinching, understanding the interior was never the rooms. Tomas leaves for the coast with Nadia's address in his pocket; Vera agrees, for the first time, to speak the old language with Petra weekly. Beat: release; endings distributed among the ensemble.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Epilogue, months later. Petra finishes her stalled translation, dedicating it 'to the kept.' She begins teaching the old language to a neighborhood kid whose family lost theirs, starting with the word that means kept, held, owed. Final image: a new inventory notebook, its first page listing things that will be said. Beat: belonging rebuilt as practice, not inheritance.
